newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.S. faces annual U.N. roasting over Cuba embargo.
newsitem.headline: U.S. faces annual U.N. roasting over Cuba embargo.

text.p: The United States, for the fifth year in a row, faces a roasting in the General Assembly on Tuesday over its three-decade-old economic embargo of Cuba.
The criticism is likely to be harsher than ever because of the latest U.S. legislation, known as the Helms-Burton act, which is aimed at penalising those who trade with Cuba.
The critics, including U.S. allies as well as adversaries, object to what they regard as a violation of their own and other countries' sovereignty subjecting them to U.S. laws and regulations.

The vote on an assembly resolution last year calling for an end to the embargo against Cuba was 117 to 3, with 38 abstentions. Only Israel and Uzbekistan lined up with the United States in opposing the resolution.
The vote on a similar draft in 1994 was 101 to 2, with 48 abstentions.

The Helms-Burton act allows U.S. citizens who were Cuban nationals before the 1959 Communist revolution to sue in U.S. courts foreign companies or individuals that "traffic" in property confiscated by the government of President Fidel Castro.

It also allows U.S. visas to be denied shareholders and officers of foreign firms operating these properties in Cuba. This provision has already been used to punish a Canadian mining company and a Mexican telecommunications firm.

The law was enacted when anti-Castro sentiment was runnning high in Washington after Cuban fighter planes last February shot down two light planes belonging to a Miami-based Cuban exile group, killing all four people aboard.

General Assembly action against the U.S. embargo in previous years was spurred by such legislation as the so-called Torricelli act of 1992, which made foreign subsidiaries of American firms liable to prosecution for trading with Havana and barred ships from U.S. ports for six months after they called at a Cuban port.

A Cuban-sponsored resolution, similar to those adopted in the past by overwhelming majorities, again calls on all states to "refrain from promulgating and applying laws and measures" that affect the sovereignty of other countries.

Without mentioning the United States by name, it "once again urges states that have (applied) and continue to apply such laws and measures to take the necessary steps to repeal or invalidate them as soon as possible."

The draft expresses concern that since the adoption of similar resolutions each year since 1992, further measures continue to be promulgated "aimed at strengthening and extending the economic, commercial and financial embargo against Cuba."
About 20 countries, including both Cuba and the United States, are expected to speak in the assembly debate.
